title: When Can You Seal New Concrete (and Why Waiting Matters)
metaTitle: When to Seal New Concrete in Ontario
metaDescription: New driveways and patios need time to cure before sealing. Here is the reasoning behind the wait and how it applies to new builds in Southwestern Ontario.
excerpt: Sealing new concrete too early can trap moisture and cause problems that show up later. Here is why the curing period matters and how to plan around it.
heroAlt: Freshly poured concrete driveway in a new London Ontario subdivision waiting to fully cure before sealing
keyTakeaways: New concrete needs time to cure fully before sealing, since sealing too early can trap moisture still working its way out of the slab.
New subdivisions around London and Woodstock see a steady stream of freshly poured driveways, making curing time a common question for homeowners moving into new builds.

body.text: Homeowners in new subdivisions across London and Woodstock often reach out shortly after their driveway or patio is poured, wanting to protect the fresh concrete right away. That instinct is understandable, but new concrete needs time before it is ready for sealing, and understanding why helps explain why a contractor recommending patience is giving good advice rather than delaying unnecessarily. This guide covers what is actually happening inside a curing slab, how long that process typically takes, and how to plan sealing around it in a way that protects the concrete rather than compromising it.
Why new concrete cannot be sealed right away

Concrete does not simply harden and stop changing once it is poured and finished. It continues to cure for an extended period, during which excess water used in the mixing process gradually evaporates out of the slab and the concrete continues to gain strength. Sealing traps whatever moisture is still present at the time of application at or near the surface. If a sealer is applied before that internal moisture has had a chance to escape, it can become trapped beneath the cured sealer film, leading to problems that range from a hazy or cloudy appearance to blistering, where pockets of trapped moisture push the sealer film up and away from the concrete surface. Neither of these is something that fixes itself; both typically require stripping the sealer and starting over, which costs more time and money than simply waiting the appropriate curing period in the first place.
How long new concrete needs before sealing

The general guidance for new concrete is that it needs roughly a month of curing time before sealing, though this can vary somewhat based on weather conditions, the concrete mix used, and how the slab was finished. Concrete poured during warm, dry weather tends to cure a bit more predictably than concrete poured during cooler or wetter stretches, since curing speed is affected by temperature and humidity. This is one of the reasons the free site assessment matters for new construction specifically: rather than applying a blanket rule to every slab, an actual look at the concrete and knowledge of when and under what conditions it was poured gives a more accurate picture of whether it is ready.

This waiting period is a common source of questions for homeowners moving into new builds in London, Woodstock and surrounding growth areas, where a driveway might be poured weeks or months before the rest of landscaping and exterior work wraps up. It is worth building the sealing timeline into your overall move-in plan rather than treating it as an afterthought once everything else is finished.
What happens if you seal too early

Beyond the moisture-trapping issue described above, sealing concrete before it has cured sufficiently can interfere with how well the sealer bonds to the surface in the first place. A slab that is still releasing moisture and alkalinity from the curing process presents a different surface chemistry than fully cured concrete, which can affect adhesion and lead to a sealer coat that wears unevenly or fails prematurely compared to one applied to properly cured concrete. Given that TriCity Concrete Sealing backs every job with a 5-year workmanship warranty, applying sealer to concrete that has not cured properly is not something to rush into, since the goal is a coating that performs for years, not one that needs redoing within the first season.

The wait for new concrete to cure is not about caution for its own sake. Sealing too early is one of the more common causes of avoidable problems like blistering and cloudy finishes on otherwise brand-new concrete.
How the curing window interacts with sealing weather

Once new concrete has cured sufficiently, actual sealer application still depends on the same weather conditions that apply to any sealing project: dry surfaces and temperatures roughly between 10 and 30 degrees Celsius, which in Southwestern Ontario generally means spring through fall. This means the timing of a new slab's first sealing depends on both when it was poured and when the curing period lines up with suitable weather. A driveway poured in early summer might be ready to seal by late summer with the season still cooperating. A driveway poured in October, closer to the edge of the construction season, might finish its curing period well into a stretch of weather too cold for sealing, pushing the first application into the following spring. This is another reason a straightforward conversation with the crew doing the assessment is more useful than trying to calculate an exact date independently.
New builds and clay soils

New subdivisions across the London and Woodstock area are frequently built on clay soils, which shift more than sandier or more stable soils through seasonal moisture changes and freeze-thaw cycles. This does not change the fundamental curing timeline for the concrete itself, but it is part of why a properly sealed driveway matters over the following years: a slab on shifting clay subsoil benefits from the added protection against water infiltration that a good sealer coat provides, since keeping water out of the concrete's pore structure reduces one of the contributing factors to freeze-thaw stress on top of whatever ground movement is already happening beneath the slab.
What to do while you wait

The curing period does not mean a new driveway or patio needs to sit untouched and unprotected with no plan in place. It is a reasonable time to book a free site assessment in advance, so that once the concrete has cured sufficiently and the weather cooperates, sealing can be scheduled without another round of back-and-forth. It is also a good opportunity to think through finish choice, whether that is matte, semi-gloss or gloss, since the decision benefits from seeing the actual finished concrete rather than photos alone. Our guide comparing matte, semi-gloss and gloss finishes is a useful starting point for that conversation, and the driveway and stamped concrete service pages at /services/driveway-sealing and /services/stamped-concrete-sealing cover what the sealing process itself looks like once the slab is ready.
New concrete versus recoating existing concrete

It is worth distinguishing between sealing brand-new concrete for the first time and recoating a surface that has already been sealed before. The curing considerations covered above apply specifically to new, unsealed concrete, since the entire concern is moisture still leaving a slab that has never had a protective coating on it. A driveway that was sealed years ago and is due for its regular reseal is in a completely different situation: the concrete itself finished curing long ago, and the only real timing question is weather and surface dryness at the time of application. If you have a mix of new and existing concrete on the same property, such as a new driveway apron poured alongside an older, already-sealed walkway, it is worth mentioning both during the assessment so each surface can be scheduled appropriately rather than treated the same way by default.
Common mistakes homeowners make with new concrete

A few patterns come up repeatedly with new builds. The most common is simply underestimating the curing period and wanting to seal within the first week or two after the pour, often out of a reasonable desire to protect a brand-new investment right away. Another is assuming that because concrete looks and feels hard almost immediately, it must be fully cured, when in reality surface hardness and complete internal curing are not the same thing. A third is scheduling sealing for late in the fall specifically because the driveway just passed its curing milestone, without checking whether the weather will still be within the 10 to 30 degree Celsius range needed for proper application. Working with a contractor who flags these issues before they become problems, rather than one who will seal on request regardless of timing, tends to produce a better long-term result.
Planning sealing for a new build

If you have a new driveway, patio or walkway going in, the most practical approach is to note the pour date, plan for roughly a month of curing time as a baseline, and reach out for a free site assessment as that period nears its end. faq.q: How long does new concrete need to cure before sealing?
faq.a: A general guideline is roughly a month, though this can shift based on weather conditions and the concrete mix used. A free site assessment can confirm whether a specific slab is ready rather than relying on a fixed rule alone.

faq.q: What happens if concrete is sealed too early?
faq.a: Sealing before the slab has fully cured can trap moisture still working its way out of the concrete, which can lead to a hazy or cloudy finish or blistering, where trapped moisture pushes the sealer film away from the surface.

faq.q: Can I seal my new driveway myself right after it is poured to protect it?
faq.a: It is not recommended. New concrete needs its full curing period before sealing regardless of who applies the sealer, since the underlying issue is moisture still leaving the slab, not the application method.

faq.q: Does the season a driveway is poured affect when it can be sealed?
faq.a: Yes. Sealing requires temperatures roughly between 10 and 30 degrees Celsius and dry surfaces, so a slab poured late in the fall may finish curing during weather too cold to seal, pushing the first application to the following spring.

faq.q: Do new subdivisions in London and Woodstock have any special considerations?
faq.a: Many new builds in the area sit on clay soils, which shift more with seasonal moisture and freeze-thaw cycles. This does not change the curing timeline but is part of why sealing matters for protecting the slab once it is ready.
